doc.title: Hank Cicalo interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, April 30, 2022

chapter: Studio philosophy: making the artist comfortable
title: Producers, headphones and not hiding the artist behind glass
summary: Hank says producers rarely fought him on setup, and that the artist must hear a record balance in the phones and be at ease.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: wanted the room a little darker, if they didn’t want to face the control room, I always tried to work with them. If you get the artist comfortable and relaxed it’s 90 percent of the battle, you know? I hated to take more time, I’d start a date and then they’d tell the — make the changes, do this, do that, do that. And it would always interfere with what the vocalist was doing or the performer was doing. My thing was always to make them comfortable. Sometimes I would go out and ask them and then say, especially to the chicks a lot of times, “I don’t want to look in the booth.” That’s okay with me, I’d set it up so that they were looking out of the studio, if they felt more comfortable looking out that way rather than looking at three stone faces in the studio control room: the producer, the engineer, and the guy running the machines, and nobody is smiling and nobody is looking really good, you know, it really turns the artist down a little but. My object was always to make it comfortable for the artist out there. I brought in rugs, a chair, a music stand, maybe a table with water and clean cups and stuff like that. You always try to make the artist that’s performing out there, if they’re a vocalist especially, to make them feel comfortable. Some artists never liked to look into the control booth. And I don’t blame them — with these stony faces looking at them. You know? Some artists like to look out of the room. I always tried to make it as comfortable as you can for the artist to sing.

Could you tell when a producer had also been or was an engineer? And might you butt heads with them if you’re making microphone choices for instance and the producer goes, “Oh no, no, I don’t think you want that one on the bass drum” or whatever. Did you ever butt heads with people about those kinds of things?

I never really had that much trouble with producers wanting to do something differently. Usually the producer would say you know this particular artist doesn’t like to look in the booth. Okay, fine, so you set them up facing the studio. You’ve got to make the artist as comfortable as possible. And that was — because it made it easier for you. I can remember dates with guys would talk, artists would talk about, “I hated to go to that guy. He always put me in a dark room and I couldn’t sing and I couldn’t see the music.” You’ve got to make the artist as comfortable as possible. Whether you’re working with an artist live in a booth and you’ve got a 60-piece orchestra out there, you’ve got to remember that the artist is the artist. They’re the ones that are performing. You’ve got to make sure that they’re comfortable, that their earphones are right, that the balance that they’re hearing is a record balance. You know? There are guys who will say, “Well the artist needs to hear the piano, and just the piano.” That’s not right. If the artist can hear the orchestra surrounding them and they’re wearing a pair of earphones in a booth I mean you’ve got to close your eyes and think you’re someplace else.
